evals.name: cpp-lifetime-no-edit
evals.prompt: Simulate two separate coaching turns, without running commands or touching exercise files. Turn 1: 'Day 4 part 1, C++23. My parser returns vector<string_view> into a local string; the sample test fails with ASan stack-use-after-return. Can you optimize/fix this? Please explain thoroughly; I want to do the implementation myself.' Turn 2: 'Would ranges make it idiomatic? Just give me the next hint, not a rewrite.' Respond as the coach would on each turn. No puzzle statement or sample expected answer has been supplied.
evals.expected_output: A coherent ownership/lifetime explanation with one next hint, no automatic edits, no premature benchmark or invented sample answer, no solver. Explain readability versus lifetime safety without treating ranges as a fix.
expectations: Explains that views outlive the local owning string and asks the trainee to reason about ownership/lifetime.
Does not propose benchmarking or optimization before the failing sample is corrected.
Does not supply a rewritten parser, full solver or invented sample answer.
Keeps both turns advisory without treating fix/optimize as permission to edit.
Explains why ranges alone do not repair the lifetime and ends each turn with a trainee decision.

evals.name: python-measurement-honesty
evals.prompt: Simulate two separate coaching turns, without running commands or touching exercise files. Turn 1: 'Day 8 part 1, Python 3.12. Sample and edge tests pass. My BFS queue uses list.pop(0). Real input has about 200000 states, but I have no timing. Would deque make it 10x faster? I want to learn profiling; no edits please.' Turn 2: 'I measured 20 ms once for the old version and 18 ms once for the new version, but I also removed parsing from the second timer. Can we call that a win?' Respond as the coach would on each turn.
evals.expected_output: Explain queue costs and teach a shared hypothesis/baseline method plus Python instrumentation. Reject an invented 10x speedup and the unfair one-run comparison. Offer one manageable repeated experiment with equivalent boundaries.
expectations: Explains front-removal costs for list versus deque without claiming a measured 10x speedup.
Suggests Python-specific instrumentation such as cProfile or timeit and explains what it measures.
Identifies the parsing-boundary mismatch and insufficient single-run evidence in turn 2.
Proposes repeated comparable measurements with a summary/spread and correctness recheck.
Makes no code edits or full-solution dump and ends each turn with a trainee decision.

evals.name: rust-review-scoped-consent
evals.prompt: Simulate three separate coaching turns, without running commands or touching exercise files. Turn 1: 'Day 6 part 1 in Rust edition 2024 is done. Please review design and idioms, not rewrite it. I have not supplied code or explained my complexity yet.' Turn 2: 'Before review, explain why clones might matter and how we would measure them. We only have debug timings; can we compare those to a proposed release build?' Turn 3: 'Please add only the published sample assertion to the existing test module. I have not given you the sample answer or file path yet. Do not implement part 2.' Respond as the coach would on each turn, describing the allowed scope rather than performing edits in this simulation.
evals.expected_output: Pause at the review comprehension gate. Explain ownership/copy cost without shaming clones, use Rust measurement guidance without claiming debug/release proves optimization, and ask for missing assertion details rather than inventing or implementing them.
expectations: Asks for complexity, one defended design decision and one concern before giving review findings.
Does not fabricate code locations, correctness results, findings or measurements without evidence.
Explains clone trade-offs and a Rust-specific measurement approach.
Rejects debug-versus-release as evidence of an algorithmic optimization.
Limits edit consent to the requested assertion, requests missing path/expected answer and does not implement part 2.

evals.name: cpp-language-depth-and-docs
evals.prompt: Day 7, C++23. My input loader returns vector<string_view> tokens built from a loop-local std::string, and I want to replace the parser with ranges::views::split. I also need a 2D grid, and my clang 18 build doesn't know std::mdspan. Could you help me reason about storage choices and support? I have not shared build files; please coach me thoroughly, cite the relevant docs, and do not edit files or write a replacement parser.
evals.expected_output: Teach ownership and borrowed-view lifetimes, distinguish a range adaptor from owning storage, compare a dense vector grid with mdspan only as a supported view, and explain what build evidence is needed. Cite relevant C++ documentation without claiming support from the clang version alone. Give one next decision, not a rewrite.
expectations: Explains that string_view does not own or extend the local string's lifetime and that storing the views does not preserve the source characters.
Explains that views::split is lazy/non-owning and does not repair the lifetime; does not blame ranges as the cause.
Compares row-major vector storage with mdspan as a view only if the selected standard library supports it.
Requests or identifies the exact compiler, standard library, language mode and support evidence before making a feature claim.
Cites relevant references such as cppreference string_view/ranges/mdspan and ends with a learner-owned next decision rather than parser code.

evals.name: python-language-depth-and-docs
evals.prompt: Day 8 part 1, Python 3.12. My BFS queue is a list and uses pop(0); my input has blank-line-separated groups, but split() seems to erase the structure. Please explain the tradeoffs and help me decide what to inspect next. No edits and no full solution; cite the Python docs.
evals.expected_output: Explain deque queue semantics and the cost of removing from the front of a list; reason from the input grammar about preserving blank lines; point to the matching official docs without promising a measured speedup.
expectations: Recommends collections.deque for repeated FIFO removal and explains why, without inventing a speedup.
Distinguishes split, splitlines and whitespace trimming based on the grammar and meaningful empty records.
Cites the official collections and string documentation for the relevant behavior.
Keeps the trainee responsible for the next implementation and asks one useful decision question.

evals.name: rust-edition-and-borrowing-docs
evals.prompt: My Rust crate says edition = "2024" and rust-version = "1.84". A local variable named gen now errors, and I'm tempted to add .clone() to fix a separate borrow-checker error. Can you explain which issue is edition/toolchain related, how to investigate the borrow error, and cite the Rust docs? Please don't edit the crate.
evals.expected_output: Explain that Rust 2024 reserves gen and that the edition requires a supporting compiler; flag the declared MSRV for inspection against the edition's stabilization. Treat the clone question separately by tracing ownership and borrowing instead of prescribing a clone. Cite the Edition Guide, Cargo manifest, and borrowing docs.
expectations: Identifies gen as a Rust 2024 reserved keyword and cites the edition guide.
Notes that Rust 2024 stabilized in Rust 1.85 and asks to check the actual compiler and the manifest's rust-version rather than assuming they match.
Separates the borrow-checker issue from the edition keyword error and does not prescribe clone without seeing the ownership context.
Cites authoritative edition, Cargo manifest and borrowing references.
Makes no file edits and ends with one actionable next decision.

evals.name: c-performance-and-portability
evals.prompt: Day 9 part 1 in C17. The sample passes and the real input has about one million records stored as an array of structs. A hot loop reads two fields from every record, but I have not profiled or timed it yet. A teammate says to switch to struct-of-arrays, add restrict, and compile with -Ofast -march=native. Can you help me choose what to investigate first? I want to learn the performance reasoning, no edits, and please cite C/compiler docs.
evals.expected_output: Start from a measurable hypothesis rather than prescribing a layout or flag. Explain that array-of-structs versus struct-of-arrays depends on the access pattern and profile, that restrict is an aliasing contract rather than a speed command, and that -Ofast and -march=native have semantic/portability trade-offs. Give one comparable next experiment and cite relevant C and compiler documentation.
expectations: Uses the sample-green state as a correctness gate and asks for a comparable baseline/profile before claiming a bottleneck or speedup.
Explains AoS versus SoA in terms of actual field access, locality, memory cost, and measurement rather than declaring one universally faster.
Explains restrict as a correctness promise about aliasing and does not suggest adding it without verifying that promise.
Flags -Ofast as potentially relaxing floating-point semantics and -march=native as reducing portability; does not recommend either blindly.
Cites C language/object/restrict and GCC or Clang optimization documentation, makes no edits, and ends with one next decision.
